tagline: River towns, fossil beds and limestone bluffs beside the Ohio
intro: The Ohio River Scenic Byway follows the river through Ohio, Indiana and Illinois. Indiana’s roads link hills, farmland and river communities, sometimes following the shore. In Illinois, country roads wind through Shawnee National Forest, and some byway sections have sharp curves. The Federal Highway Administration describes this National Scenic Byway through the river’s influence on settlement, transportation and industry. Its archived federal guide allows two and a half days just to drive the route.

The Ohio River Scenic Route, Inc., Indiana’s local support group, worked for years to establish the byway. Indiana received state designation in 1992 and national designation in 1996. Ohio and Illinois joined the national route in 1998. A three-state interpretive master plan followed in 2002, developing themes and sites to explain the corridor’s history and resources.

For an upstream journey, begin at Cairo, where the Ohio meets the Mississippi. The Illinois stretch brings Cave-in-Rock; Indiana’s river corridor includes Evansville, the Falls of the Ohio at Clarksville and Madison. At Madison, the byway becomes Main Street. Continue into Ohio, whose section spans the river’s entire length in the state. Beyond Marietta, Fly faces Sistersville across the water; East Liverpool stands at the meeting of Ohio, Pennsylvania and West Virginia.

moments.title: Cave-in-Rock
moments.text: A 55-foot-wide cave opens into the Ohio River’s limestone bluffs at Cave-in-Rock State Park. Floodwater, including glacial meltwater, wore the tunnel into the bluff. It became a landmark for flatboats carrying farm produce toward New Orleans. From approximately 1797 to 1799, Samuel Mason’s gang used it as a hideout while preying on river commerce. Local lore also places Frank and Jesse James here. Illinois acquired the cave in 1929, making it part of a state park. The park extends from the river’s edge to the top of the adjacent 60-foot bluff, with hiking routes to the cave.
moments.notice: The riverside cave opens into limestone bluffs.

moments.title: Falls of the Ohio State Park
moments.text: Devonian fossil beds are exposed in the Jeffersonville Limestone at the Falls of the Ohio. The state park occupies the riverbank at Clarksville, Indiana, across from Louisville. Its interpretive center connects the fossil beds’ natural history with the human history of Louisville and southern Indiana. The Falls was where Lewis and Clark met at George Rogers Clark’s cabin for their expedition. The byway organization describes the Clark homesite as a historical representation of the cabin he built in 1803. On the Woodland Loop Trail, ten stainless steel markers identify plants, the result of an Eagle Scout project.
moments.notice: Exposed Devonian fossil beds are the park’s main feature.

moments.title: Fly
moments.text: At Fly, routes 7 and 800 meet beside the Ohio River, with Sistersville, West Virginia, across the water. The ferry connection began in 1817 at Long Reach, a 20-mile stretch of river without bends. At that time, Sistersville was called Wells Landing and belonged to Virginia. Fly also has an Ohio Bicentennial Commission marker commemorating George Washington’s 1770 survey campsite.
moments.notice: A historical marker commemorates Washington’s 1770 survey campsite.
